_doc: PHASE_2_NAVIGATION_AND_GATHERING.md §2.0 — grid extent per context.
home: fixed. Wave 17 #6 widened this from 56 to 200 (== WORLD_HALF,
data/world.ts) — the six GROUNDS a villager actually hauls to/from
(grounds.generated.json) scatter nodes up to ~197m from origin
(ironseam's far corner), so a 56m grid left every real haul entirely
outside it: findPath() bails out (out-of-bounds endpoint) and navSteer
falls back to a raw beeline for the whole trip, no road preference, no
obstacle avoidance, past the player's own buildings. 200m covers the
worst case with margin and matches the world edge, so it never falls
short again as grounds move. The regions this widened grid must NOT
make walkable are TERRAIN_REGIONS (data/terrainRegions.ts, Wave 31) —
sloped-terrain patches every home-world walker only samples the HEIGHT
of, not the slope of — so each is fenced off with its own static
'blocked' entry in navTerrain.ts's terrainExclusions, the same
mechanism that already keeps the pond unpathable, rather than by
relying on grid extent as before.
destination: window, a 96m (2x halfExtent) box that follows the player
through a template diorama rather than covering the whole declared
radius (213-352m across the nine templates — see PHASE_STATUS.md's
corrected gap #1). recentreAt is the hysteresis distance: rebuild only
once the player has moved this far from the window's current centre,
not every frame.
crypt: fixed, but sized per-descent from the generated room layout, not
from a static number here — see iteration 2.6.
maxStep is read by iteration 2.5's height rasterization, not yet by
anything in iteration 2.4 — declared here now so both iterations read
the same number rather than each hardcoding their own.
NPC_AI_SPEC §7.5 (Wave 42, A7) — separation steering for the '6-20
agents in a house' scale the spec names, where 'full RVO is overkill'
(its own words). Applied INSIDE navSteer (game/navgrid.ts) so every
existing caller (Villagers.tsx, Npc.tsx, Merchant.tsx, Locomotion.ts's
stepAgent) inherits it with no call-site rewrite beyond one optional
field (NavAgent.id, for self-exclusion).
radius 1.2 and maxPush 0.3 are §7.5's own numbers, verbatim: 'for
neighbours within 1.2m, apply a repulsion force weighted by inverse
distance, clamped to 30% of max speed so it perturbs the path rather
than replacing it'. The base direction's own magnitude (and therefore
`dist`, arrival) is never touched by any of this — only the direction
handed to navSteer's caller is perturbed, then renormalised to unit
length.
yieldPush 0.4 is this wave's own choice for the 'small per-agent
priority' §7.5 asks for (unlike radius/maxPush, the spec gives no
number for it) so two NPCs in a doorway resolve instead of
deadlocking. A cheap deterministic hash of each agent's own id
(avoidPriority(), navgrid.ts) gives every agent a stable 0..1 rank
with zero new authored data; whichever of a pair ranks higher applies
a REDUCED push (so it continues more nearly straight through the
standoff), while the lower-priority one applies the full weight — so
the one who visibly yields and sidesteps is always the lower-priority
agent, per §7.5's own wording, not whichever one happened to compute
its steering first this frame.
maxPush clamps in TWO stages, not one (navgrid.ts's own comments have
the full reasoning) — each neighbour's raw 1/d push is capped to
maxPush individually, THEN scaled by yieldMul, and only afterward is
the summed vector across all neighbours clamped to maxPush again. The
per-neighbour stage is load-bearing, not redundant: 1/d alone is
already >= maxPush (0.83) at every distance inside the whole 1.2m
radius, so clamping only the final sum (this wave's original cut)
made a lone full-weight neighbour's push and a lone reduced-weight
(yieldPush) neighbour's push saturate to the identical 0.3 for any
distance whatsoever — silently erasing the priority asymmetry for
the single most common case, the plain two-agent doorway encounter,
which needs 3+ neighbours whose raw vectors partially cancel before
the old single-stage clamp would ever let it show through. Capping
per-neighbour first restores a real, always-visible 0.3 vs 0.12
split for that common case while the second (summed) stage keeps
doing its original job of bounding a multi-neighbour crowd.
